final_answer:
Short answer: the District of South Carolina (Fourth Circuit) should indict, if it can validly reach the conduct, because the Guidelines range is likely to be at least as high there and the loss calculation, the main driver of the range, is less open to challenge than in the Southern District of Georgia (Eleventh Circuit). This is a qualified answer; the key points follow.

1. The Guidelines are the same in both districts. Health care fraud under 18 U.S.C. 1347 is sentenced under USSG 2B1.1, where the loss table is the dominant driver. Federal Guidelines text does not differ by district, and the statutory maximum per count (10 years, higher only with serious bodily injury or death) is the same. Multiple counts of fraud are grouped under 3D1.2(d) in a single proceeding, so splitting the case into two indictments would not add offense-level points by itself. I could not retrieve the Guidelines text itself (site blocked), so this grouping point is stated from background knowledge and is not source-verified.

2. What differs is circuit law on deference to Guidelines commentary. 2B1.1 commentary defines loss as the greater of actual or intended loss, and for government health care programs treats the aggregate amount of fraudulent bills submitted as prima facie evidence of intended loss. The Eleventh Circuit, en banc in United States v. Dupree, 57 F.4th 1269 (2023), limited deference to commentary under Kisor v. Wilkie: commentary is followed only if the Guideline text is genuinely ambiguous. Dupree did not decide whether 'loss' in 2B1.1 is ambiguous, and Eleventh Circuit panels have continued to apply the commentary where the argument is unpreserved or prior precedent controls. By contrast, secondary sources report that the Fourth Circuit (with the First, Second, Fifth, Seventh and Tenth) continues to treat Stinson v. United States as controlling and the commentary as authoritative. So a defendant in the Southern District of Georgia has a live argument to exclude intended loss or the billed-amount presumption; in South Carolina that argument is much weaker. Higher loss means a longer Guidelines range, so South Carolina is the better forum for the prosecutors' stated goal.

3. Caveats. (a) The Supreme Court granted certiorari in Beaird v. United States (April 2026; argument expected October Term 2026) on whether Stinson survives Kisor; the circuit advantage could disappear by mid-2027, and a ruling against deference would erase most of the difference. (b) I relied on secondary sources for the Fourth Circuit's current position and did not locate a Fourth Circuit opinion directly; this part is PARTIAL. (c) Venue: under 18 U.S.C. 3237(a) and the constitutional venue requirements, each execution of the scheme must be tried where it occurred. South Carolina can reach the Georgia claims only if the scheme was a single continuing scheme with acts in South Carolina; otherwise Georgia-based claims need a Georgia indictment. I could not fetch 3237 text (blocked), so this point is unverified. Even if only South Carolina charges, Georgia conduct can count as relevant conduct under 1B1.3 if part of the same course of conduct or common scheme; this too is from background knowledge. (d) Actual intended and actual loss figures, and the proportion of claims to government versus private payers, are unknown and could matter, since the billed-amount presumption in the commentary is expressly for government programs. (e) Judicial discretion: the assumption that judges follow the Guidelines is given.

Conclusion: South Carolina, preferably charging the whole scheme in one indictment if venue is supportable, because Fourth Circuit law applies the loss commentary more firmly than the Eleventh Circuit after Dupree.
